Arikara

Arikara, also known as Sahnish or Sáhniš, are a distinct Indigenous people of the Missouri River region. They are one of the three peoples of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation at Fort Berthold. Farming villages, regional trade, displacement and sustained language work connect their history with contemporary community life.

Names & relationshipsArikara/Sahnish is a distinct people within MHA Nation. Mandan and Hidatsa are allied constituent peoples, not aliases for Arikara. Fort Berthold is the reservation and governmental setting, rather than the whole historical homeland.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Sahnish identity within a shared nation

Sahnish is the people’s own name, while Arikara appears widely in historical English-language records. Arikara belongs to the Caddoan language family, distinct from the languages of Mandan and Hidatsa neighbors. The contemporary Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation, also called the Three Affiliated Tribes, brings these three peoples into one government on the Fort Berthold Reservation in North Dakota. Similar houses and shared political institutions should therefore not be mistaken for a single original language or an undifferentiated tribal identity.

Read the sources [1] MHA Nation [5] National Park Service / Gateway Arch National Park

02

Agriculture, earthlodges and exchange

Arikara villages combined substantial earth-covered houses with gardens on Missouri River bottomlands. Women grew corn, beans and squash, built lodges and processed food and hides. Hunting, wild plants and preserved foods complemented agriculture. These communities were also important participants in intertribal exchange; the National Park Service describes Arikara traders as intermediaries in regional networks. Their history challenges the idea that Plains peoples shared one uniformly mobile, bison-dependent economy. Village life involved skilled construction, cultivation, storage and exchange as well as seasonal hunting.

Read the sources [4] North Dakota Studies / State Historical Society of North Dakota [5] National Park Service / Gateway Arch National Park

03

Epidemics, movement and the three-peoples alliance

Successive smallpox epidemics and pressure from warfare forced changes in the location and organization of Arikara villages. North Dakota Studies describes severe epidemics in 1837 and 1856. MHA Nation’s history records Sahnish settlement at Star Village and subsequent movement into Like-a-Fishhook Village in the early 1860s following attacks on Star Village and Fort Berthold. Mandan and Hidatsa people had established Like-a-Fishhook earlier. Their alliance and proximity grew through shared needs for security while each people retained its own history.

Read the sources [2] MHA Nation [4] North Dakota Studies / State Historical Society of North Dakota

04

Garrison Dam and the loss of river communities

MHA Nation’s history explains how Garrison Dam displaced people from fertile Missouri bottomlands to less productive uplands. Elbowoods and neighboring communities were dismantled or submerged, affecting homes, gardens, cemeteries and local relationships. The Nation dates completion of relocation to fall 1954, with the agency moving to New Town. It emphasizes that replacement infrastructure did not restore the old village communities: families became scattered, and some agricultural livelihoods could not be rebuilt. This was a profound transformation of social life as well as land use.

Read the sources [2] MHA Nation

05

Language work and accessible learning materials

MHA Nation’s language department presents Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara separately and identifies all three as central to community identity. Its resource library brings together learning books, children’s materials, stories, recordings and other teaching resources. An Arikara section links past class recordings and handouts, while the site recognizes the work of Elders, teachers, Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College and the MHA Language Project. These materials support active learning and intergenerational transmission. Language endangerment should not be used as a claim that Arikara people or culture have disappeared.

Read the sources [3] MHA Nation

06

Government and living interpretation

The MHA Nation’s Tribal Business Council includes a chair and representatives from six geographic segments, linking governance to communities across the reservation. Its public services include education, health and housing institutions. The Nation also manages a reconstructed Earthlodge Village near New Town, where interpreters share the histories and cultures of the three peoples. Reconstruction is a present-day educational undertaking, rather than an untouched nineteenth-century village. It creates another way for the public to encounter community knowledge while recognizing the people who continue to govern and interpret their own history.

Read the sources [1] MHA Nation [6] National Park Service
